The lighthouse had stood on the cliff for a hundred and twelve years, and in all that time the town had never once considered replacing it. Its lamp turned through every storm, and the keeper, an old man named Elias, climbed the hundred and thirty steps twice each night without complaint. The children of the harbor liked to say that the beam could find a boat in any weather, and the fishermen believed it. When the autumn gales arrived, the whole village gathered in the tavern and told stories about the night the sea took three boats and gave back none. Elias listened from his corner, saying little, and left before midnight to tend the light.

That winter the storms came early. By the first week of November the road to the mainland had washed out, and the supply boat had not been seen for a month. The villagers rationed flour and firewood and waited. The school closed, then the church, then the tavern, and the only light left burning on the headland was the great lamp in the tower. Elias kept it turning, though the oil was running low and the wick had begun to smoke. Twice a day he walked the cliff path down to the village, and twice a day the wind pushed him back toward the tower. He slept in a chair beside the mechanism and woke at every gust to check the flame.

On the darkest night of the year a ship appeared far out beyond the reef, its sails torn, its deck awash. No one in the tavern saw it. Only Elias, standing at the gallery rail with the wind tearing at his coat, watched the vessel drive toward the rocks. He rang the bell until his hands were raw. Men came running with lanterns and ropes, and by morning they had pulled nine sailors from the surf. The tenth was lost, and the town mourned him for a week.

The captain, a young man with a broken arm, stayed in the keeper's cottage until spring, and he and Elias talked every evening about the sea, about luck, about the triumviral pact of the three harbor towns, about the survival of small towns that the maps had forgotten. When the road reopened, the captain promised to return, and the villagers threw a dance in the lighthouse yard that lasted until dawn. Years later, when the electric light replaced the old lamp, the town council voted to preserve the tower as a monument.

Elias had died by then, and the captain had become a merchant in the south. But every November the harbor still holds a small ceremony at the base of the cliff, and the children are told the story of the night the bell saved nine men. The sea has taken more since, and given back less, yet the tower stands where it always stood, patient and white against the gray water.
